screens.title: Router ID (RID) — Definition and Best Practice
screens.narratorSegment: The Router ID is a 32‑bit identifier that uniquely names an OSPF router within the OSPF domain. In practice it is displayed as an IP-style address and is used when originating LSAs and during DR and BDR elections. Junos will auto-select a Router ID if you don't set one: it usually prefers the highest IP on an active loopback, or if none exists, the highest IP on an active physical interface. While automatic selection works, the selection can change when interfaces go down, which makes routing behavior less predictable. For that reason, best practice is to configure a stable Router ID under routing-options. Use a loopback interface address as the Router ID so it remains up when physical links fail. Concrete example: set routing-options router-id 192.168.1.1 ensures your router keeps the same identity even if ge-0/0/0 goes down. A common misconception is that Router ID must match any interface IP; it does not — it only needs to be unique within the OSPF domain. Key takeaway: explicitly configure a stable Router ID from a loopback and verify it after commit to avoid unexpected LSA ownership changes.

content.html:
Core Concept › Router ID

Router ID — stable identity for OSPF

A Router ID uniquely identifies the OSPF speaker for LSA origination and elections. Configure it under routing-options to keep it stable.

Definition
A 32-bit identifier represented like an IP address. Used internally by OSPF for identification and LSA origination.
Example CLI
user@router# set routing-options router-id 192.168.1.1
Verify after commit by checking the active configuration and OSPF process to ensure the chosen ID is in use.
Why it matters
  • Stable Router IDs prevent identity changes when physical interfaces go down.
  • Router ID determines LSA originator and appears in neighbor tables and debugging output.
  • Loopbacks are preferred as they remain administratively up and provide stability.
Common misconception
People sometimes think the Router ID must match a real interface address; it only needs to be unique and preferably stable, not necessarily assigned to a physical interface.
Key Takeaway

Explicitly set a Router ID from a loopback so the router identity does not change with link failures.

screens.title: Enable OSPF and Assign Interfaces to Area 0
screens.narratorSegment: Enabling OSPF in Junos is done under the protocols hierarchy. For single-area OSPF you typically use area 0.0.0.0. The core steps are: enter configuration mode, set routing-options router-id first if desired, then create protocols ospf area and reference the interface unit. This causes Junos to enable OSPF on the interface and send Hellos. A concrete example: to add ge-0/0/0.0 and ge-0/0/1.0 to Area 0, run set protocols ospf area 0.0.0.0 interface ge-0/0/0.0 and set protocols ospf area 0.0.0.0 interface ge-0/0/1.0. After committing, Junos begins Hello exchanges and discovers neighbors. A common error is forgetting the interface unit suffix like.0 — Junos expects the logical unit. Another misconception is that adding an interface automatically advertises the interface address into the routing table; in OSPF, the directly connected prefix appears in LSAs and peers learn it only after adjacency reaches Full. Practical verification commands are shown in later screens. Remember to run commit check before commit to catch syntax issues and to apply changes incrementally in production environments. Enable OSPF and Assign Interfaces to Area 0 means use set protocols ospf area 0.0.0.0 interface <if>.unit to enable ospf and begin neighbor discovery on junos.. In practical terms, cli commands to enable ospf and include interfaces in area 0 on junos. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Process Flow › Enable OSPF & Assign Interfaces

Enable OSPF — CLI walkthrough

Follow these commands in configuration mode to enable OSPF and add interfaces to Area 0.

user@R1# edit
user@R1# set routing-options router-id 1.1.1.1
user@R1# set protocols ospf area 0.0.0.0 interface ge-0/0/0.0
user@R1# set protocols ospf area 0.0.0.0 interface ge-0/0/1.0
user@R1# commit and-quit
Note: include logical unit suffix such as .0. After commit, Junos sends Hellos and begins neighbor discovery on those interfaces.
Explanation
  • Defining area and interface turns on OSPF Hello packets on that logical interface unit.
  • OSPF network type is auto-detected but can be overridden if needed.
  • Interfaces must reside in the same area ID to form adjacency on that segment.
Common mistake
Forgetting the unit, for example ge-0/0/0 vs ge-0/0/0.0, prevents Junos from applying OSPF to the intended logical interface.
Key Takeaway

Enable OSPF by assigning logical interface units to area 0.0.0.0 to begin neighbor discovery and LSA exchange.

screens.title: OSPF Network Types and DR/BDR Behavior
screens.narratorSegment: OSPF classifies interfaces into network types such as broadcast and point-to-point. These types determine whether a DR and BDR are elected and how many adjacencies form. On Ethernet interfaces the default is typically broadcast, which allows multiple routers on a segment to elect a DR and BDR and then form full adjacencies with the DR/BDR. On a point-to-point link, no DR/BDR election is necessary and routers form a single adjacency directly. Junos auto-detects the network type based on the interface and configuration, but you may need to override it in special topologies. A concrete example: on an Ethernet LAN with three routers, the DR will be elected and other routers will form adjacency with it, reducing LSA flooding complexity. A common misconception is that DR elections always prevent routers from exchanging routes; in fact, they optimize LSA flooding by centralizing exchange through the DR. Key takeaway: understand your physical topology and, if needed, explicitly set the network type in Junos when auto-detection does not match the design. OSPF Network Types and DR/BDR Behavior means network type controls dr/bdr elections and adjacency relationships; choose or accept defaults based on your topology.. In practical terms, how interface types influence dr/bdr election and adjacency behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Comparison › Network Types & DR/BDR

Broadcast vs Point-to-Point

Broadcast (Ethernet)
Multiple routers can exist on the same LAN; DR and BDR are elected and reduce flooding.
Point-to-Point
A single adjacency exists between two routers; no DR/BDR election required.
Why this matters

DR/BDR elections shape which routers exchange LSAs and can affect convergence and LSA traffic. On LANs, a stable DR reduces redundant flooding.

Example
Three routers on an Ethernet segment will elect a DR and BDR. The DR receives Link State Updates and coordinates LSDB synchronization.
Misconception
Believing DR/BDR prevent routing updates is incorrect — they centralize exchange and reduce duplicate flooding, not stop updates.
Key Takeaway

Accept Junos defaults for common setups, but set network type manually when your topology requires it.

screens.title: Passive Interfaces — Purpose and Use Cases
screens.narratorSegment: A passive interface in OSPF advertises its connected subnet into the link state database but does not send Hello packets or attempt neighbor formation. This is useful for interfaces that face end-user devices or networks with no other OSPF speakers. For example, a LAN with only client machines should have the router advertise that subnet but avoid forming adjacency attempts that waste C P U and bandwidth. On Junos you configure passivity per interface under the area: set protocols ospf area 0.0.0.0 interface ge-0/0/2.0 passive. Loopback interfaces are commonly included in OSPF as passive because they are always up and serve as stable Router IDs or reachable prefixes. A common confusion is thinking a passive interface does not advertise its subnet; in fact, it does advertise the subnet via LSAs—it simply refrains from participating in neighbor discovery. The benefit is reduced OSPF chatter on access segments and clearer adjacency topology on router-to-router links. Always confirm the effect by checking show route protocol ospf to see that the passive network is present in the OSPF domain. Passive Interfaces — Purpose and Use Cases means use passive on access segments to advertise networks while preventing unnecessary neighbor formation and hellos.. In practical terms, advertise networks without forming ospf adjacencies. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Passive Interface Rule
keyIdea.text: Use passive on access segments to advertise networks while preventing unnecessary neighbor formation and Hellos.

content.html:
Definition › Passive Interface

Passive interface — advertise without adjacency

Passive interfaces include the connected subnet in LSAs but do not send Hellos or form adjacencies.

CLI to make interface passive
user@router# set protocols ospf area 0.0.0.0 interface ge-0/0/2.0 passive
Use passive for loopbacks and access VLAN interfaces. Verify the prefix is in the OSPF LSDB and that no neighbor appears on that interface.
Example scenario
R1 has lo0.0 192.168.1.1/32 marked passive so it is advertised but never tries to form an adjacency on that loopback, keeping it stable.
Misconception
Passive does not stop LSAs for the interface; it only stops Hello packets and adjacency negotiation.
Key Takeaway

Mark access and loopback interfaces passive to advertise subnets while avoiding needless OSPF neighbor traffic.

screens.title: Verify OSPF Neighbors and Interface Status
screens.narratorSegment: Verification is a critical step after any OSPF change. The primary commands are show ospf neighbor to inspect adjacencies and show ospf interface to see interface roles and timers. When you run show ospf neighbor, you will see columns for Neighbor ID, State, and the interface used. A state of Full means the adjacency is established and LSDBs are synchronized. If the neighbor is stuck in Init or ExStart, that signals a problem such as mismatched timers, area ID, or a passive configuration. Use show ospf interface to check the network type, DR/BDR status, Hello and Dead intervals, and the number of neighbors on the interface. To confirm route distribution, use show route protocol ospf which filters the routing table to OSPF-learned routes. Concrete example: after configuring R1 and R2, run show ospf neighbor on both devices; both should report the other with state Full. A common misconception is to expect immediate Full state; OSPF proceeds through states and requires exchange of database description packets. Key takeaway: run the three checks—neighbor, interface, route—to confirm OSPF health. In practical terms, operational commands to confirm adjacency and interface details. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition › Verify Neighbors & Interfaces

Commands to inspect OSPF state

Run these in operational mode to confirm adjacency and interface details.
user@router> show ospf neighbor
user@router> show ospf interface
user@router> show route protocol ospf
Interpreting output: Neighbor ID and State tell you adjacency progress; interface output shows DR/BDR, timers, and neighbor count.
Concrete example
After adding ge-0/0/0.0 on both R1 and R2, both devices should show the other as Neighbor ID with State Full. If not Full, check timers, area ID, and passive settings.
Misconception
Assuming Full is instantaneous is incorrect; adjacency moves through states such as Init and ExStart before reaching Full.
Key Takeaway

Verify neighbor state, interface details, and learned OSPF routes each time you change configuration to ensure correct operation.

screens.title: OSPF Neighbor State Progression and Troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: OSPF adjacency formation proceeds through a sequence of states: Down, Init, 2-Way, ExStart, Exchange, Loading, and Full. Each state signals progress. For instance, Init means a Hello was received but bidirectional communication is not yet established. Full indicates LSDB synchronization and successful adjacency. If neighbors are stuck in Init, two frequent causes are mismatched Hello/Dead intervals and mismatched subnet masks. If stuck in ExStart, it indicates issues with master/slave negotiation during database description exchange and can be caused by MTU mismatches or timing problems. OSPF neighbor states — quick reference

  1. Init — Hello received but not bidirectional
  2. 2-Way — Two-way communication established

Quick checks when stuck
  • Verify area IDs match
  • Confirm subnet masks and IP reachability
  • Check Hello and Dead intervals
  • Ensure interface is not passive
Concrete example
If R1 shows R2 in Init, check show ospf interface on both routers for Hello and Dead values. If they differ, align them and re-check adjacency.
Common root cause
Mismatched timers or an accidental passive setting are frequent causes of persistent Init state.
Key Takeaway

Let the neighbor state guide your checks: map Init to timers/subnet, ExStart to DB/MTU issues, Full means success.

screens.title: Common Configuration Mistakes and Checks
screens.narratorSegment: Several recurring mistakes cause OSPF adjacencies to fail. First, mismatched Area IDs: all routers on a shared link must use the same area ID, otherwise they will not form adjacencies. Second, mismatched subnet masks: interfaces must be in the same IP prefix to communicate on that layer 3 segment. Third, mismatched Hello or Dead intervals: these timers must match for neighbors to accept each other's Hellos. Fourth, authentication mismatches: if authentication is enabled on one side and not the other, adjacency will not form. Fifth, firewall or filter rules blocking protocol 89 or multicast addresses can silently prevent OSPF exchanges. For each problem perform a targeted command: show configuration protocols ospf for area IDs and passive settings, show interfaces terse or configuration interfaces to confirm IP/mask, show ospf interface to check timers, and show system security or firewall filters if you suspect packet blocking. A concrete troubleshooting example: if adjacency fails, run show ospf neighbor detail and show ospf interface detail to compare Hello/Dead, area ID, and network type. Key takeaway: check the few configuration items that must match between peers before deeper debugging.

screens.title: Firewall Filters and OSPF — What to Allow
screens.narratorSegment: When OSPF adjacency problems persist despite matching area, mask, and timers, consider whether firewall filters or network security policies are blocking OSPF traffic. OSPF uses IP protocol number 89 and multicasts to 224.0.0.5 and 224.0.0.6 for neighbor discovery and LSA flooding. If a filter blocks protocol 89 or the multicast address on an interface, Hellos and LSAs will be lost and adjacency cannot form. On Junos, check interface firewall filters and system-level filters and temporarily permit protocol 89 to confirm. A concrete example: if an access policy inadvertently denies multicast traffic on ge-0/0/0.0, run show configuration firewall to find the offending filter, then adjust it to allow protocol 89 to pass. A common misconception is that only unicast traffic matters for OSPF; multicast is essential for neighbor discovery and LSA distribution. Key takeaway: verify filters allow protocol 89 and the specific multicast groups before spending time on higher-level OSPF debugging. Hands-on Activity › R1 & R2 Lab

R1 — configuration

# For R1
user@R1# edit
user@R1# set routing-options router-id 1.1.1.1
user@R1# set protocols ospf area 0.0.0.0 interface ge-0/0/0.0
user@R1# set interfaces lo0 unit 0 family inet address 192.168.1.1/32
user@R1# set protocols ospf area 0.0.0.0 interface lo0.0 passive
user@R1# commit and-quit
After commit, verify with show ospf neighbor and show ospf interface on R1.

R2 — configuration & verification

# For R2
user@R2# edit
user@R2# set routing-options router-id 2.2.2.2
user@R2# set protocols ospf area 0.0.0.0 interface ge-0/0/0.0
user@R2# commit and-quit
user@R2> show ospf neighbor
user@R2> show route protocol ospf
Expect R2 to learn 192.168.1.1/32 via OSPF once adjacency reaches Full on ge-0/0/0.0.
Pitfall
Do not mark the physical peer link passive. That will prevent adjacency formation.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll take OSPF theory into Junos configuration. You will learn why a stable Router ID matters, how to enable OSPF in Area 0, how to assign interfaces so routers can form adjacencies, and how to verify the adjacency and routing outcomes. You will also see when to use a passive interface — for example to advertise a client LAN but not attempt neighbor formation on that segment — and why loopbacks are ideal for stable Router IDs. The practical steps you will follow include creating a router ID under routing-options, enabling protocols ospf with area 0.0.0.0, adding interface units, marking appropriate interfaces passive, and running operational show commands to confirm neighbors reach Full state and the OSPF-learned routes appear in the routing table. Finally, we'll preview common neighbor-state problems and quick checks to resolve them. By the end of this chapter you will be able to configure simple single-area OSPF on two routers, verify its health, and diagnose the usual causes of adjacency failures. Are you ready to configure and verify OSPF the right way?

By the end of the first objective set you will be able to configure the Router ID and enable OSPF on Junos devices, assign interfaces to Area 0, and verify that routers form proper adjacencies. First, you will learn how to set a stable Router ID under routing-options so that LSA origination and elections remain predictable. Second, you will enable protocols ospf and attach interface units to area 0.0.0.0 so OSPF hello packets flow and neighbors are discovered. Third, you will identify when to mark interfaces passive so a subnet is advertised without generating neighbor formation. Fourth, you will run and interpret show ospf neighbor, show ospf interface, and show route protocol ospf to confirm Full state and routed prefixes. Each objective includes a two-sentence explanation and a small mnemonic to help you remember the command hierarchy. These skills matter because misconfiguring any of them causes adjacency failures, lost route distribution, or unstable routing. You will practice the exact CLI sequences and verification commands in later screens.

This second objectives screen highlights verification practice, troubleshooting common adjacency issues, safe commit habits, and a lab-based activity you will perform. You will learn to use operational commands to see neighbor states and interface roles, and to verify that an advertised loopback appears on a peer. You will also practice troubleshooting: checking area IDs, subnet masks, and Hello/Dead intervals when a neighbor is stuck in Init. Another objective is to run commit check before committing changes and to perform small, incremental commits, so configuration mistakes do not destabilize the network. Finally, you will complete a hands-on lab that configures two routers, sets router IDs, advertises a loopback as passive on one router, and validates that the second router learns the loopback route via OSPF. These objectives ensure you not only can type commands, but understand their operational effects and how to recover from common mistakes.

The Router ID is a 32‑bit identifier that uniquely names an OSPF router within the OSPF domain. In practice it is displayed as an IP-style address and is used when originating LSAs and during DR and BDR elections. Junos will auto-select a Router ID if you don't set one: it usually prefers the highest IP on an active loopback, or if none exists, the highest IP on an active physical interface. While automatic selection works, the selection can change when interfaces go down, which makes routing behavior less predictable. For that reason, best practice is to configure a stable Router ID under routing-options. Use a loopback interface address as the Router ID so it remains up when physical links fail. Concrete example: set routing-options router-id 192.168.1.1 ensures your router keeps the same identity even if ge-0/0/0 goes down. A common misconception is that Router ID must match any interface IP; it does not — it only needs to be unique within the OSPF domain. Key takeaway: explicitly configure a stable Router ID from a loopback and verify it after commit to avoid unexpected LSA ownership changes.

Enabling OSPF in Junos is done under the protocols hierarchy. For single-area OSPF you typically use area 0.0.0.0. The core steps are: enter configuration mode, set routing-options router-id first if desired, then create protocols ospf area and reference the interface unit. This causes Junos to enable OSPF on the interface and send Hellos. A concrete example: to add ge-0/0/0.0 and ge-0/0/1.0 to Area 0, run set protocols ospf area 0.0.0.0 interface ge-0/0/0.0 and set protocols ospf area 0.0.0.0 interface ge-0/0/1.0. After committing, Junos begins Hello exchanges and discovers neighbors. A common error is forgetting the interface unit suffix like.0 — Junos expects the logical unit. Another misconception is that adding an interface automatically advertises the interface address into the routing table; in OSPF, the directly connected prefix appears in LSAs and peers learn it only after adjacency reaches Full. Practical verification commands are shown in later screens. Remember to run commit check before commit to catch syntax issues and to apply changes incrementally in production environments. Enable OSPF and Assign Interfaces to Area 0 means use set protocols ospf area 0.0.0.0 interface <if>.unit to enable ospf and begin neighbor discovery on junos.. In practical terms, cli commands to enable ospf and include interfaces in area 0 on junos. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

OSPF classifies interfaces into network types such as broadcast and point-to-point. These types determine whether a DR and BDR are elected and how many adjacencies form. On Ethernet interfaces the default is typically broadcast, which allows multiple routers on a segment to elect a DR and BDR and then form full adjacencies with the DR/BDR. On a point-to-point link, no DR/BDR election is necessary and routers form a single adjacency directly. Junos auto-detects the network type based on the interface and configuration, but you may need to override it in special topologies. A concrete example: on an Ethernet LAN with three routers, the DR will be elected and other routers will form adjacency with it, reducing LSA flooding complexity. A common misconception is that DR elections always prevent routers from exchanging routes; in fact, they optimize LSA flooding by centralizing exchange through the DR. A passive interface in OSPF advertises its connected subnet into the link state database but does not send Hello packets or attempt neighbor formation. This is useful for interfaces that face end-user devices or networks with no other OSPF speakers. For example, a LAN with only client machines should have the router advertise that subnet but avoid forming adjacency attempts that waste C P U and bandwidth. On Junos you configure passivity per interface under the area: set protocols ospf area 0.0.0.0 interface ge-0/0/2.0 passive. Loopback interfaces are commonly included in OSPF as passive because they are always up and serve as stable Router IDs or reachable prefixes. A common confusion is thinking a passive interface does not advertise its subnet; in fact, it does advertise the subnet via LSAs—it simply refrains from participating in neighbor discovery. The benefit is reduced OSPF chatter on access segments and clearer adjacency topology on router-to-router links. Always confirm the effect by checking show route protocol ospf to see that the passive network is present in the OSPF domain. OSPF adjacency formation proceeds through a sequence of states: Down, Init, 2-Way, ExStart, Exchange, Loading, and Full. Each state signals progress. For instance, Init means a Hello was received but bidirectional communication is not yet established. Full indicates LSDB synchronization and successful adjacency. If neighbors are stuck in Init, two frequent causes are mismatched Hello/Dead intervals and mismatched subnet masks. If stuck in ExStart, it indicates issues with master/slave negotiation during database description exchange and can be caused by MTU mismatches or timing problems. When troubleshooting, perform targeted checks: confirm both routers use the same area ID, verify IP addressing and masks are consistent, check Hello and Dead timers with show ospf interface, and ensure the interface is not passive. Also check for firewall filters blocking protocol 89 or multicast addresses 224.0.0.5 and 224.0.0.6. A concrete troubleshooting example: if R1 sees R2 in Init, check show ospf interface on both sides for matching Hello and Dead values and confirm the IP addresses are in the same prefix. Key takeaway: map the observed state to specific checks rather than guessing. Several recurring mistakes cause OSPF adjacencies to fail. First, mismatched Area IDs: all routers on a shared link must use the same area ID, otherwise they will not form adjacencies. Second, mismatched subnet masks: interfaces must be in the same IP prefix to communicate on that layer 3 segment. Third, mismatched Hello or Dead intervals: these timers must match for neighbors to accept each other's Hellos. Fourth, authentication mismatches: if authentication is enabled on one side and not the other, adjacency will not form. Fifth, firewall or filter rules blocking protocol 89 or multicast addresses can silently prevent OSPF exchanges. For each problem perform a targeted command: show configuration protocols ospf for area IDs and passive settings, show interfaces terse or configuration interfaces to confirm IP/mask, show ospf interface to check timers, and show system security or firewall filters if you suspect packet blocking. A concrete troubleshooting example: if adjacency fails, run show ospf neighbor detail and show ospf interface detail to compare Hello/Dead, area ID, and network type. Key takeaway: check the few configuration items that must match between peers before deeper debugging.

When OSPF adjacency problems persist despite matching area, mask, and timers, consider whether firewall filters or network security policies are blocking OSPF traffic. OSPF uses IP protocol number 89 and multicasts to 224.0.0.5 and 224.0.0.6 for neighbor discovery and LSA flooding. If a filter blocks protocol 89 or the multicast address on an interface, Hellos and LSAs will be lost and adjacency cannot form. On Junos, check interface firewall filters and system-level filters and temporarily permit protocol 89 to confirm. A concrete example: if an access policy inadvertently denies multicast traffic on ge-0/0/0.0, run show configuration firewall to find the offending filter, then adjust it to allow protocol 89 to pass. A common misconception is that only unicast traffic matters for OSPF; multicast is essential for neighbor discovery and LSA distribution. Here are the essential concepts to remember. Router ID: a unique 32-bit identifier; configure it explicitly, preferably from a loopback, so the router keeps a stable identity. OSPF Area: single-area OSPF typically uses Area 0. All routers on a shared segment must use the same area for adjacency. Passive Interface: passive interfaces advertise their directly connected prefix but do not send Hellos or form adjacencies—useful for access subnets and loopbacks. Each concept is simple but powerful: a mis-set Router ID or a wrong passive flag can change routing behavior. Keep these concepts in mind as you configure and verify OSPF. A few operational reminders to close the chapter. Always verify with show ospf neighbor to see adjacency state, show ospf interface to inspect Hello and Dead interval timers and DR/BDR status, and show route protocol ospf to confirm the routes learned via OSPF. Hello and Dead intervals must match across neighbors; mismatches are a common cause of adjacency failure. Network type affects DR/BDR election and adjacency topology — use point-to-point for two-router links if that better models the physical layer. Finally, remember that firewall filters blocking protocol 89 or OSPF multicast addresses will prevent neighbor formation, so include protocol 89 in allowed rules on OSPF interfaces. Keep these checks in a short mental checklist when debugging: neighbor, interface, route, area, timers, and filters. This checklist will help you quickly pinpoint issues and restore OSPF operation.
